title: The nuns first (Prouille, 1206)
hook: Dominic's first community was of women

segments.voice: Yesterday, preaching poor: horses sent home, and the harder memory of the courts that came later. Your line was poor preachers. What did you leave behind before you spoke? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-one.

Ask who the first Dominicans were, and the picture may be of men: friars in white and black, walking to the cities, preaching in the squares. But go back to the south of France, to a small place called Prouille, at the foot of a hill. Before there was an Order of Preachers, before the pope had approved anything, Dominic and his bishop Diego gathered a household there. Not of preachers. Of women. They prayed, they worked, they lived together behind walls. Today, the community that came before the friars.
screen: `FRIARS IN WHITE AND BLACK?` → `A SMALL PLACE CALLED PROUILLE.` → `NOT PREACHERS. WOMEN.`

segments.voice: Why women? The reason is in Jordan of Saxony's account. In that region, he says, some families who were noble but poor had handed their daughters to the Cathars to be raised and taught, because they could not provide for them. When women like these came back to the Catholic faith, they had nowhere to go. So Diego and Dominic founded a monastery at Prouille to receive them. It became the first house of what grew into the Dominican family. The friars came after. That's an odd start for an order of preachers. Dominic's first community didn't preach in the streets at all. It prayed. Dominicans sometimes speak of their nuns' prayer as going before the friars' words. A preacher walking into a hostile town at dawn has someone already praying for him. And the Gospel has its own women who came first in their own way. Luke tells how women traveled with Jesus and the Twelve: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna, and others, in the Douay-Rheims, "who ministered unto him of their substance." They paid for the road. Luke places them at the cross, and at the empty tomb. At Prouille, too, women are the first chapter. Before the order had a name, a rule or a pope's approval, it had a house of women praying.
screen: `DAUGHTERS WITH NOWHERE TO GO.` · `A MONASTERY AT PROUILLE.` · `PRAYER GOES BEFORE THE PREACHING.` · `WOMEN WHO PAID FOR THE ROAD.` · then, large: `WHO MINISTERED UNTO HIM OF THEIR SUBSTANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank praying women. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a woman who prayed for you, or simply held you in her thoughts, before you knew it: a grandmother, a mother, an aunt, a teacher, a neighbor, a nun in a school you went to. Let her face come. Then, like Joanna and Susanna giving of their substance, remember one concrete thing she gave: a meal, a ride, an evening, a few dollars, a word at the right time. Breathe in, and hold that one gift. If you pray, you can thank God for her by name. If you don't, just say her name and the gift, slowly, to yourself. The bell holds the time.
The nuns first. At Prouille, Dominic's first community was a house of women at prayer, before there were any friars. Today's word.
Your line: the nuns came first. Today, tell one woman who prayed for you, or carried you, that you noticed. A text will do. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Dominican nuns live enclosed lives of prayer, study and work in monasteries, praying especially for the preaching of the friars; Dominicans honor Prouille as the first house of their family.

notes: Claims rule: the title's date is not repeated in the voice.

Jordan's account paraphrased: Diego founded the monastery at Prouille to receive noble women whose parents, because of poverty, had given them to the heretics to be educated and raised. Confirm, and whether Diego or Dominic should be given more credit (the voice says 'Diego and Dominic').
'It became the first house of what grew into the Dominican family' follows the index hook ('Dominic's first community was of women'). Confirm.
'In some tellings of Christian history, women are the footnote' is a general claim; flag for the editor.
Original: 'Sancta Praedicatio' (the Holy Preaching) as a name for the early Prouille/Fanjeaux community: confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 8:3 to confirm.

Editor pass: teach no longer opens 'Jordan of Saxony explains why' (third Jordan opener in a row); the families' reason now follows the review note (poverty) instead of an unsourced 'home and an education'; cut the general claim 'in some tellings of Christian history, women are the footnote' (flagged by the writer; 'footnote' also used in 1230) and the 'hidden heart ... holds them up' line, which repeated 1215's hidden-prayer angle; the practice's widening to unnamed women praying unseen (repeats 1215's practice) and 'thank you into the room' (repeats 1228) replaced with remembering one concrete gift, tied to Luke 8:3. The myth reveal, which also said 'a home and an education', was updated to match.
